newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy economy sluggish, exports, imports fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy economy sluggish, exports, imports fall.

text.p: The Italian economy ended 1996 on a low note, with industrial output in decline and exports and imports doing worse than expected, national statistics office Istat said on Friday.

Italy's gross domestic product (GDP) rose just 0.8 percent in 1996 compared with a jump of three percent the year before, according to provisional Istat figures, which were in line with official forecasts.
The country is striving to get its economy in shape for the 1999 launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU).

In the final three months of last year, the economy fell 0.1 percent against the third quarter -- the second time negative quarterly growth was registered during 1996. On the year-on-year level, GDP rose a meagre 0.5 percent.
"This GDP report has confirmed that the economy entered the first quarter of 1997 with very weak momentum," said Ilaria Fornari, economist with bank JP Morgan in Milan.

"The medium-term outlook remains one of very stagnant, or at best very slow growth," she added, with a host of industrial and consumer surveys pointing to no turnround in the business cycle until the second quarter at the earliest.
An Istat spokesman said the dip in quarterly GDP was largely caused by a decline in industrial output, which was only partially offset by a slight improvement in the service sector.

The statistics office gave no further details but figures released last week showed industrial production tumbling an unexpected 3.1 percent year-on-year in December. Full GDP data for 1996 will be presented to parliament by the end of March.
"Industrial output seems to have gone very badly in the fourth quarter but this is not a novelty," said Marco Ratti, an economist with Banca Commerciale Italiana in Milan.
However calendar changes also had an impact.

The Istat data is seasonally adjusted, but does not take into account working days. There were two more working days in the fourth quarter of 1996 against the corresponding period of 1995, but two fewer working days compared to the third quarter.
The Istat spokesman said exports were worse than forecast, while imports were sharply down year-on-year.

Lira gains towards the end of 1996 put a brake on the long-running export boom, which had been ignited by the dramatic devaluation of the Italian currency at the end of 1992 after it crashed out of the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
The lira returned to the ERM last November.
Economists believe imports were hit by a decline in equipment investment and flat domestic consumption.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has forecast that the economy will grow between one and 1.5 percent this year, scaling down confident, original projections of two percent growth.
"Almost everyone is forecasting another year of very slow growth, much near one percent than 1.5 percent," Ratti said.
The economy has been hurt by an increasingly tough series of budgets, which are designed to prepare Italy for EMU.
Prodi's centre-left government introduced a 62.5 trillion lire ($37 billion) deficit cutting budget at the end of last year and has promised more belt-tightening for the spring.

"Clearly the bigger the budget, the smaller your economic growth," Ratti said. Italian Treasury undersecretary Laura Pennacchi said on Wednesday that the planned mini-budget would be for between 14 and 15 trillion lire.
